clue.text: Fly to French city? This'll bring you closer still

parts.note: to fly is to zoom, move very fast
Lens is a city in northern France

explanation.surface: A traveller wonders about flying to a French city and getting closer still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'still' is not 'even yet' but a still photograph: the lens brings the subject of the shot closer.
explanation.definitionFit: A camera attachment with variable focal length magnifies the subject of a photograph, bringing it apparently nearer.

clue.text: Loaded up, left note, set out

indicators.note: the letters are laid out afresh in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone loaded up, left a note and set off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set out' rearranges UP, L and NOTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Loaded is slang for very wealthy, which is what opulent means.

clue.text: Film from the thirties or the present age

explanation.definitionFit: Chaplin's 1936 comedy has this title, and the phrase also names the contemporary period.

clue.text: Opening like St. Peter's gates, but less quietly

indicators.note: the quiet letter is subtracted from the word

parts.note: heaven's gates are the pearly gates
P is piano, the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: Heaven's gates opening, but more loudly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' is an adjective, as in the opening stages.
explanation.definitionFit: Opening as an adjective means at the start, like the early stages of something.

clue.text: Philosopher rushes up with lightweight answer

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: nips means rushes, as in nips to the shop
oz, ounce, is a small weight

explanation.surface: A philosopher hurries upstairs with a slight reply.
explanation.definitionFit: Baruch Spinoza was a 17th-century Dutch rationalist thinker.

clue.text: Show surprise

definitions.meaning: to show up or arrive, as a verb phrase
an unexpected event, a noun in British use

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means arrive or appear; as a hyphenated British noun it means an unexpected result.

clue.text: Look like the next scene in the film

definitions.meaning: to resemble a parent or relative

definitions.text: the next scene in the film
definitions.meaning: a take is a filmed shot, and the following one comes after

explanation.definitionFit: To resemble a relative is to take after them; read literally, it is the film shot that follows.

clue.text: Regularly drain old port

indicators.note: every other letter of drain is taken

explanation.surface: Advice to drain old port wine at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: Even letters of DRAIN give RI. 'port' looks like the wine but is the Brazilian city.
explanation.definitionFit: Rio de Janeiro is a major Brazilian seaport.

clue.text: Downfall of spaniel, for one without a lead, it's kept in

indicators.note: the word in is held inside the rest
the first letter is dropped, as a dog off its lead

parts.note: a spaniel is a kind of gundog
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spaniel off its lead brings ruin, so it is kept indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without a lead' drops the first letter, as a dog let off its lead, leaving UNDOG; 'it's kept' means the word in is held inside that.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's undoing is the cause of their ruin or downfall.

clue.text: Fail fully to exploit deal for radio play

parts.note: to fail to milk something fully is to undermilk it
deal is pine or fir timber, a kind of wood

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone failed to make the most of a business deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Dylan Thomas's famous 1954 play for voices was written for BBC radio.
explanation.definitionFit: Dylan Thomas's work about a Welsh village is the best-known drama written for broadcast on the wireless.

clue.text: Yankee's fish shop

parts.note: a Yankee is a British accumulator bet on four horses
a ray is a flat fish

explanation.surface: An American's fish shop, as if naming a store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shop' is the slang verb, to inform on someone; a Yankee is a British betting term for a multiple bet.
explanation.definitionFit: To shop someone is British slang for informing on them, which is to give them away treacherously.

clue.text: Say, Samson the sailor goes back wearing glasses to 7

indicators.note: the glasses have something inside them, as a person wears clothes

parts.note: a pair of spectacles looks like two letter Os

indicators.note: the sailor's word runs backwards

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor
the answer to 7 down, a Brazilian port

explanation.surface: Samson the sailor heads back to port wearing spectacles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes back' makes the sailor RAT, which 'wearing' sets inside the spectacles. Samson is Handel's choral work, not the strongman; 7 refers to the answer to 7 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Handel's Samson is an example of a large sacred choral work for voices and orchestra, hence 'Say'.

clue.text: Boss is to get them in

definitions.meaning: to boss is to give commands, a verb
to get the drinks in for everyone at the pub

explanation.definitionFit: As a phrasal verb it means boss about; read literally it is buying a round of drinks.

clue.text: Say, credit a paper that ministers need

parts.note: to say is to state
CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit
FT is the Financial Times, a British newspaper

explanation.surface: Advice to praise a newspaper that government ministers need on side.
explanation.definitionFit: Skill in managing affairs of government is what a cabinet member must possess.

clue.text: Thinking about nothing having drunk gin and tonic

indicators.note: the rearranged drink goes round the zero
the gin and tonic are mixed up as if drunk

parts.note: O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Thinking of nothing after a gin and tonic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' mixes the drink's letters into CGNITION, which goes 'about' the zero. The surface toper is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Cognition is the mental process of knowing and reasoning, that is, thinking.

clue.text: Is very keen on flat, say

definitions.meaning: in slang, someone who ... something likes it a lot
British slang for lodgings, of which a flat is an example

explanation.definitionFit: In slang it means likes greatly; as a British noun it means rented rooms or lodgings.

clue.text: Mollusc left in river

indicators.note: the letter for left sits inside the river's name

parts.note: the Cam is the river through Cambridge

explanation.surface: A shellfish abandoned in a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A bivalve shellfish is one kind of mollusc.

clue.text: Butcher's to get rid of grime at last, having received fine

indicators.note: the losing word takes the fine word inside

parts.note: to get rid of something is to lose it
OK means fine

indicators.note: the final letter of grime is used

explanation.surface: A butcher getting rid of the last of the grime after a fine.
explanation.walkthrough: Butcher's is rhyming slang: butcher's hook means look.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang a butcher's is a quick look, a peek.

clue.text: Attack insurance worker who's run off to gamble everything

parts.note: to go for someone is to attack them

indicators.note: run goes off, departing from the worker's title

parts.note: an insurance broker arranges policies; who's ties the worker to what follows
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: An attack on an insurance agent who has fled to place a big bet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' removes R (run) from BROKER, leaving BROKE; 'who's' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means risking all one's resources on a single venture.

clue.text: More familiar person up for the first time?

definitions.text: person up for the first time
definitions.meaning: a first-year student, up at university

explanation.definitionFit: It means cheekier, and is also British for a first-year student; going 'up' means arriving at university.

clue.text: The nick's revolting food prepared here

indicators.note: the letters rise up in revolt and change order

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Prison food so bad it causes a riot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The nick' is British slang for prison; 'revolting' rearranges THE NICK.
explanation.definitionFit: Meals are cooked in this room of a house or restaurant.

clue.text: Church accepts prison-reforming scheme

indicators.note: the church abbreviation takes the other letters inside it

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: the letters of prison are reformed into a new order

explanation.surface: A church takes on a project of prison reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reforming' makes ONSPIR from the prison, and the church abbreviation 'accepts' it.
explanation.definitionFit: To conspire is to plot together, which is to scheme as a verb.

clue.text: Hook for one awfully good carpet

parts.note: pi is slang for pious or sanctimonious, too good by half
to carpet someone is to scold them, an old sense of rate

explanation.surface: Something hooked as an example of a terribly nice rug.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Hook of Peter Pan is the example; 'carpet' and 'rate' are both verbs meaning reprimand.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Hook is a famous fictional example of a buccaneer.

clue.text: Adverts for pants

definitions.meaning: pants as a verb, breathes heavily

explanation.definitionFit: Puffs are flattering promotions, and someone who puffs is panting.

clue.text: Good group of clubs want the respectable and rich

parts.note: straight can mean honest and conventional
flush means well supplied with money

explanation.surface: Fine golf or social clubs are after decent wealthy members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clubs' is the card suit: five clubs in sequence make a strong poker hand.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker, five cards of one suit in sequence, such as clubs, form a very strong hand.

clue.text: Grass, speed but not ecstasy

indicators.note: the ecstasy letter is taken away

parts.note: rate means speed
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Drug talk: grass and speed but no ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' is the slang verb or noun for an informer, not the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Grass and rat are both slang for an informer.

clue.text: Employee of the Church Times involved in attack

indicators.note: the times sign is placed within the attack phrase

parts.note: to set on someone is to attack them
X is the multiplication sign, read as times

explanation.surface: A Church Times staffer caught up in an assault.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'Church Times', the newspaper, but 'Church' belongs to the definition and 'Times' is X.
explanation.definitionFit: A church officer who looks after the building and graveyard is a paid worker of the church.

clue.text: Local leader ignored by head of state

indicators.note: the first letter of the head of state's title is dropped

parts.note: a president is a republic's head of state

explanation.surface: A local leader is snubbed by the head of state.
explanation.definitionFit: A local is someone who lives in the area, an inhabitant.
